speaker: Rory Sutherland
title: Marketing Expert: The Playbook Behind Every Great Campaign | Rory Sutherland
question: In consumer technology, why do genuinely innovative new products actually require more marketing than familiar ones?
guest: Just as a camera has a default mode, the human default mode is: do what I did before, and do what everybody else does. That's a very rational default mode—there's nothing silly about it in terms of our evolutionary brain architecture. What you've done before and what everybody else does may not be optimal, but it's much less likely to be catastrophic. What I realized thirty-five years into working in this business is that, as a consequence, big, innovative new ideas don't require less marketing—they require more. At the initial stages, you're asking someone to do something that nobody else has done, and you're asking them to do something they haven't done before. Both of those create a kind of disquiet. Providing people with conviction and reassurance, in the early stages of a technology, quite often happens one-to-one. For me, it was my brother—who's an astrophysicist and knows all the maths about kilowatt hours—who provided me with the reassurance to buy my first electric car. If he hadn't bought one first, I wouldn't have bought one.

points.core: Human defaults favor repeating past habits to avoid catastrophic downside risk.
points.note: Accept: evolutionary or rational habit bias ("do what I did before") minimizing worst-case failure rather than optimizing upside. Do not credit: generic claims that people are lazy or resist change without the downside-protection mechanism.

points.core: Buyers also default to copying peers as a rational safety heuristic.
points.note: Accept: social proof or herding ("do what everyone else does") as a low-risk default. Do not credit: vague mentions of peer pressure or trends.

points.core: Innovative products trigger heightened anxiety by violating both defaults simultaneously.
points.note: Accept: novel products forcing buyers to do something neither they nor others have done before, creating acute disquiet or perceived risk that superior specs alone do not erase. Do not credit: generic statements that new products are unfamiliar or confusing.

points.core: Early adoption often depends on one-to-one reassurance from trusted peers.
points.note: Accept: personal conviction, word-of-mouth validation, or reassurance from a knowledgeable friend/family member overcoming initial adoption anxiety. Do not credit: generic recommendations to use influencer marketing or testimonials without the trust/reassurance mechanism.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because a truly new product has to create its own demand before it can capture any. A familiar product slots into a category people already understand: buyers know what a phone or laptop is for, so marketing only has to argue "ours is better." An innovative product has no such mental category. People don't know what it is, what problem it solves, or why they'd want it, and they often don't feel the problem at all until shown the solution.

That means marketing must do extra jobs: educate the market, demonstrate use cases, and justify a change in behavior. Innovations also carry higher perceived risk and switching costs (new habits, uncertain reliability, missing ecosystem), and people tend to overvalue what they already use, so the benefits must be made vivid to overcome inertia.

Finally, there's the adoption gap described by Everett Rogers and Geoffrey Moore: enthusiasts will seek out novelty themselves, but mainstream buyers need social proof, clear positioning, and reassurance before they move. Without sustained marketing, even superior technology stalls at the early-adopter stage.

points.why: The response describes inertia and switching costs without explaining how repeating past behavior protects against severe downside.
The response mentions social proof without explaining why following others’ choices is a low-risk default.
The response identifies perceived risk but does not trace it to buyers simultaneously departing from their own habits and from what others do.
The response says mainstream buyers need reassurance without identifying one-to-one reassurance from a trusted peer as a driver of early adoption.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Familiar technology benefits from built-in comprehension: consumers already understand what a smartphone or laptop does, why they need one, and how to compare options, allowing marketing to focus narrowly on better features or lower prices. Genuinely innovative products lack that mental shortcut, forcing companies to build an entire category before selling the device itself. Marketers must surface problems people may not realize they have, show how an unfamiliar tool fits into daily life, and establish a sense of value without existing price or performance benchmarks.

Moreover, true innovation demands habit change, and consumers naturally overweight the friction of abandoning comfortable routines relative to unproven benefits. Novel hardware or software also carries heightened perceived risk, as mainstream buyers worry about steep learning curves, ecosystem compatibility, and whether a new format will endure or quickly become obsolete. Extensive, sustained marketing is required to bridge that gap—using repeated education, hands-on demonstrations, cultural storytelling, and social proof to turn initial confusion and skepticism into everyday confidence.

points.why: The response attributes sticking with habits to the friction of switching and leaves out the role of familiar behavior in protecting against severe downside.
The response lists social proof as a marketing tactic without explaining why buyers treat copying peers as a safer default.
The response discusses habit change and perceived product risks without linking heightened anxiety to the simultaneous absence of personal and peer precedent.
The response gives no account of how one-to-one reassurance from a trusted peer helps an early adopter commit.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Familiar products slot into a category people already understand. A buyer already knows what a smartphone or laptop is for, so the marketing only has to say "ours is better or cheaper." A genuinely new product has more work to do. It has to create demand, not just capture it.

First, it has to teach. Consumers often don't recognize the problem the product solves, have no frame of reference for judging it, and can't picture it fitting into their routines. Early smartwatches and VR headsets struggled with exactly this.

Second, it has to overcome resistance to change. John Gourville's research on the "9x effect" found that consumers overvalue what they already have by about three times, while companies overvalue their innovation by about three times. That gap has to be bridged through persuasion, demonstration and reassurance about risk, learning costs and switching costs.

Third, adoption spreads unevenly. Diffusion-of-innovation theory and Geoffrey Moore's "chasm" describe how enthusiastic early adopters differ from the pragmatic mainstream, who want proof, social validation and complete solutions. Reaching them takes sustained effort, and products with network effects often need heavy investment just to reach critical mass.

points.why: The response describes overvaluing what one already owns but does not explain how repeating past behavior protects against severe downside risk.
The response says mainstream buyers want social validation but does not explain that buyers default to copying peers because it feels safer.
The response discusses unfamiliarity and switching costs but does not connect heightened anxiety to acting without either personal precedent or peer precedent.
The response mentions reassurance in general but does not explain how one-to-one reassurance from a trusted peer gives early buyers confidence to adopt.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Familiar products benefit from existing mental models and built-in demand. When a company releases a faster laptop or a sharper television, consumers already know what the product does, how it fits into their lives, and how to judge whether it is worth buying. Marketing only needs to differentiate it from competitors.

Genuinely innovative technology faces a much harder job: it has to create a category from scratch. Before a company can sell the product, it must educate people on what it even is, reveal a problem they may not realize they have, and show why the new solution beats their current workaround. Innovation also demands behavioral change. Asking consumers to abandon familiar habits, learn a new interface, and risk money on an unproven idea triggers strong status quo bias. To overcome that skepticism and move beyond niche early adopters into the mainstream, companies must invest heavily in storytelling, demonstrations, and social proof until the unfamiliar feels intuitive and indispensable.

points.why: The response links an unproven purchase to status quo bias but leaves unexplained how repeating past behavior protects against severe downside.
The response lists social proof as a marketing tactic without explaining why buyers copy peers to reduce risk.
The response attributes skepticism to changing habits and risking money, leaving out the added anxiety of acting without peer precedent.
The response recommends social proof in general and gives no account of how personal reassurance from a trusted peer helps someone adopt early.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Familiar products benefit from what buyers already know. If you’re shopping for a new phone, you know what it does, when you might need one, and which features matter to you. The company mostly has to explain why you should choose its model.

A genuinely new product has to earn a place in the buyer’s life first. People need to understand what it does, recognize a problem it solves, and see why it’s worth the cost, effort, or risk of changing their habits. The more unfamiliar the product, the harder it is for buyers to make those connections on their own. That’s why demonstrations, trials, and relatable examples matter so much. The company has to build demand for the category as well as for its own product.

points.why: The response mentions the risk of changing habits but omits why repeating past behavior is a rational default that limits severe downside.
The response does not identify copying peers as a way buyers reduce perceived risk.
The response describes unfamiliarity and the perceived risk of changing habits but misses the heightened anxiety that comes when buyers lack both personal and peer precedent.
The response suggests demonstrations, trials, and relatable examples but omits the role of one-to-one reassurance from a trusted peer in early adoption.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A familiar product starts with a customer who already understands what it does and why they might want it. Marketing can focus on why this version is worth choosing. With a genuinely new product, there’s an earlier question to answer: “Why would I use this at all?”

Even when the technology is impressive, its value may be hard to see until someone sees it solve a problem they recognize. And if adopting it means learning a new skill or changing a habit, sticking with the familiar feels easier. That’s why innovation often takes more marketing work. A clear demonstration makes the benefit concrete, a trial lets people judge whether it’s worth the effort, and seeing others use it reduces uncertainty.

points.why: The response attributes sticking with familiar products to ease and leaves out protection against serious downside risk.
The response says observing others reduces uncertainty but stops short of identifying imitation as buyers’ default safety strategy.
The response discusses habit change and uncertainty separately and never links heightened anxiety to the simultaneous absence of personal and peer precedent.
The response mentions observing other users but gives no account of direct reassurance from a trusted person helping someone adopt early.
